blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Bayesian statistics treats an unknown parameter as uncertain and describes that uncertainty with a probability distribution. A prior distribution states what is believed about the parameter before the new data. Bayes’ theorem (recall §5.5) combines it with the likelihood of the data (recall §13.1) to give the posterior distribution: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. A 95% credible interval is a range that contains the parameter with 95% posterior probability, given the prior and the model.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The methods of this book so far are frequentist: probability is a long-run frequency over repeated samples (recall §6.5 and the careful reading of a confidence interval in §7.2). Bayesian inference starts instead from probability as a degree of belief (recall subjective probability, §5.1.3) and updates it with data.

You have already done a Bayesian update. In §5.5.3, a referral-clinic patient with pre-test probability 30% had a positive test with LR+ 9.5, and the post-test probability became 80.3%: pre-test odds 0.4286 × 9.5 = 4.07, probability 4.07/5.07 = 0.803. The pre-test probability is the prior, the likelihood ratio carries the data, and the post-test probability is the posterior. The same logic applies to a whole range of parameter values.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Beta–binomial updating. Let p be a prevalence. A convenient prior is the Beta(a, b) distribution, a distribution on 0 to 1 with density proportional to p^(a−1)(1 − p)^(b−1) and mean a/(a + b). It behaves like a earlier “successes” and b earlier “failures”. The binomial likelihood of x cases in n (recall §5.7.1.2) is proportional to p^x(1 − p)^(n−x). Multiplying:

posterior ∝ p^(a+x−1)(1 − p)^(b+n−x−1), which is Beta(a + x, b + n − x).

The posterior mean (a + x)/(a + b + n) is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample proportion x/n, with weights (a + b) and n.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Last year’s survey in a block suggested that about 40% of pregnant women attending a PHC were anaemic, with about the information of 50 women: prior Beta(20, 30). This year 30 of 60 women tested are anaemic (x/n = 0.50).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Prior mean: 20/50 = 0.40 (95% prior interval 0.27 to 0.54).
  2. Posterior: Beta(20 + 30, 30 + 30) = Beta(50, 60). Mean 50/110 = 0.455, between the prior 0.40 and the data 0.50; the prior carries weight 50/110 = 45%.
  3. 95% credible interval: the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles of Beta(50, 60), from software, are 0.363 to 0.548. By hand, a Normal approximation works well here: the posterior SD is √[50 × 60 ÷ (110² × 111)] = 0.047, and 0.455 ± 1.96 × 0.047 = 0.362 to 0.547.
  4. P(prevalence > 50% | data, prior) = 0.17.
  5. With a flat prior, Beta(1, 1), the posterior is Beta(31, 31): mean 0.50 and 95% credible interval 0.377 to 0.623, almost the same as the frequentist Wilson interval for 30/60 (0.377 to 0.623; recall §7.2.4). With little prior information, the two approaches give similar numbers but different interpretations.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
a <- 20; b <- 30                     # prior: Beta(20, 30), mean 0.40
x <- 30; n <- 60                     # new data: 30 of 60 anaemic
c(prior = a/(a + b), posterior = (a + x)/(a + b + n))
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a + x, b + n - x)   # 95% credible interval
# same data, flat Beta(1, 1) prior
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), 1 + x, 1 + n - x)
# P(prevalence > 50% | data, prior)
1 - pbeta(0.5, a + x, b + n - x)
    prior posterior 
0.4000000 0.4545455 
[1] 0.3628812 0.5477760
[1] 0.376968 0.623032
[1] 0.1690927

The lines are steps 1–2, 3, 5 and 4. qbeta gives quantiles of the Beta posterior and pbeta its cumulative probability; nothing is simulated, because the conjugate posterior has a known form.

points.html: The prior matters, so it must be stated and defended. It may come from earlier studies or expert opinion, or be deliberately vague (“uninformative”). Report a sensitivity analysis with other priors, as in step 5.

A credible interval is a probability statement about the parameter, conditional on the prior and the model. “Given this prior and this binomial model, there is a 95% probability that the prevalence lies between 36% and 55%.” A frequentist 95% CI does not allow that sentence (recall §7.2). If the prior or model is wrong, the credible interval is wrong too.

Evidence accumulates naturally. Today’s posterior can be tomorrow’s prior. Frequentist methods also accumulate evidence, through cumulative meta-analysis (§15.7) and group-sequential trial designs, but Bayesian updating expresses it more directly.

Uses in health research include hierarchical models (for example, small-area estimates of district prevalence that borrow strength from neighbouring districts, as random effects do in §15.2.3), adaptive trial designs, and the interpretation of diagnostic tests. Most real models need simulation (Markov chain Monte Carlo) rather than the closed form above; a full treatment is beyond this book.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 15.13

questions.prompt: With the prior Beta(20, 30), a survey in a second PHC finds 12 of 40 pregnant women anaemic. Give the posterior distribution and its mean. Is the posterior mean closer to the prior mean or to the sample proportion, and why?
questions.answer: Posterior = Beta(20 + 12, 30 + 28) = Beta(32, 58). Mean = 32/90 = 0.356 (95% credible interval 0.261 to 0.457 from software; by hand, SD = √[32 × 58 ÷ (90² × 91)] = 0.050, and 0.356 ± 1.96 × 0.050 = 0.257 to 0.454). Prior mean 0.40; sample proportion 12/40 = 0.30. The posterior mean is a weighted average with weights 50 (the prior’s “sample size”, a + b) and 40 (the data): (50 × 0.40 + 40 × 0.30)/90 = 0.356. It lies slightly closer to the prior (0.044 away) than to the data (0.056 away), because the prior carries more information (50) than the new sample (40).

questions.prompt: A report says: “The 95% credible interval for the risk difference was 1% to 9%, so there is a 95% probability that the true risk difference lies in this range.” What condition must be added for the sentence to be correct? Could the same sentence be written about a 95% confidence interval?
questions.answer: It must be conditional on the prior and the model: “given the prior distribution and the statistical model used, there is a 95% posterior probability …”. With a different prior, or a wrong model, the interval and the probability change. The sentence cannot be written about a frequentist 95% CI: there the 95% refers to the method (95% of intervals built this way, over repeated samples, contain the true value), and the parameter is not given a probability distribution.

questions.prompt: A clinician’s pre-test probability of tuberculous lymphadenitis is 10%. A test with LR+ 6 is positive. Compute the post-test probability, and name the prior, the likelihood and the posterior in this calculation.
questions.answer: Pre-test odds = 0.10/0.90 = 0.111. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 6 = 0.667. Post-test probability = 0.667/1.667 = 0.40. Prior: the pre-test probability (10%, or odds 0.111). Likelihood: the likelihood ratio, P(positive | disease)/P(positive | no disease) = 6, which carries the evidence of the result. Posterior: the post-test probability, 40%.
